In the first hour or so of the game, I was pretty underwhelmed by just how basic the combat and gameplay felt.
Instead of aiming down the scope or having an alternate weapon-fire, Luna Abyss gives you a magnetic lock-on to the nearest enemy that feels very Metroid Prime in function.
It doesn’t affect your damage or movement speed at all, you can just choose to abandon aiming and auto-fire at enemies if you please.
The aim here was likely to create a way for gunplay to feel manageable or, at worst, secondary to the moments of dodging bullets – in fairness, Saros excels thanks in part

dossier.summary: This Luna Abyss review starts where most struggle: the game is hard to describe without sounding like you're listing contradictions. It's a first-person shooter where you're not aiming at enemies so much as navigating the space around them. It's a bullet hell game where the screen isn't a flat 2D plane but a 3D environment you're physically inside. It pulls from Junji Ito's body horror visual language and Bioshock's atmospheric storytelling simultaneously, without feeling like either.

systems: The Luna Abyss review question isn't whether the genre fusion works in theory.
Players who want pattern-reading combat in a 3D horror space will find the execution matches the ambition; players expecting a conventional FPS will bounce off the difficulty immediately.
Combat fuses FPS mechanics with incoming projectile patterns that require active first-person dodging
The combat is where the genre merge gets unusual.
Not a ramp, not a tutorial gauntlet: just combat that expects you to start parsing dense pattern information from the first fight.
The specific skill the game demands is pattern reading in three dimensions.

It's a bullet hell game where the screen isn't a flat 2D plane but a 3D environment you're physically inside.
It pulls from Junji Ito's body horror visual language and Bioshock's atmospheric storytelling simultaneously, without feeling like either.

TL;DR: Luna Abyss is a first-person bullet-hell shooter where survival is about navigating 3D projectile space rather than aiming, wrapped in Junji Ito-style body horror and Bioshock-flavored atmosphere.
It's a genre hybrid that mostly pulls off its contradictions: the moment-to-moment dodging is tense and the world is oppressive in the right way.
It asks for patience with its pacing, so it suits players who want atmosphere-driven bullet hell over a fast arcade shooter.
The Luna Abyss review question isn't whether the genre fusion works in theory.
It's whether the full game delivers on what a demanding audience is willing to follow.

Science fiction has always treated the moon as a place of mystery.
Sometimes it becomes a frontier, sometimes a warning, and sometimes a mirror reflecting humanity back at itself.
Luna Abyss takes that fascination and reshapes it into something unsettling.
It is an artificial mimic world, hiding ancient ruins, forgotten technology, and the remains of a civilisation swallowed by catastrophe.
You play as Fawkes, a prisoner sentenced to descend beneath Luna’s surface to recover lost technology from a colossal megastructure known only as the Abyss.
Every step is monitored by your artificial prison overseer, Aylin, whose calm guidance slowly reveals layers of uncertainty beneath her composed exterior.
As Fawkes pushes deeper into the ruins of Greymont and confronts the echoes of The Scourge, the journey becomes less about survival and more about uncovering truths long buried.
The result is a game that combines high-speed action with introspective world-building.
